parsed.explanation: No trans-specific criminal offence is in force: the 2019 same-sex provision was repealed in 2020, and the 2024 constitution declined to re-criminalise while adding privacy protection. The documented trans-relevant exposure is police use of 'breaches of modesty' charges against non-gender-conforming presentation — documented as occasional, not widespread, with a 2019 arrest-and-bribe precedent under the repealed law and 2013 arrests even before any offence existed. That enforcement lever plus thin recourse, individual harassment described as common, and a volatile legislative environment under military rule hold this below the acceptance tier. No border, facility, custody or care data exists; the state is not documented as hostile to trans people as a group. Rating 0.56: elevated-tier friction with real but occasional police exposure, not organised targeting.

entry_documents.exposure: No sourced information on passport markers, screening, or treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers at ports of entry.
entry_documents.protection: Same-sex conduct lawful; privacy provisions in the 2024 constitution.
entry_documents.interaction: Unknown document practice is an open question, not a documented exposure; discretion by individual officers cannot be assumed either way.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Police have arrested people for presentation/couple status under neutral 'modesty' laws and released them after bribes (2013, 2019); no custody-placement or detention-condition data.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: No same-sex offence is in force; most recent documented same-sex prosecution is 2019.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Arrests occurred within months of enactment, showing police willingness when a lever existed; repeal removed that lever.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: No data on facilities, bathrooms, wards or single-sex spaces.

care_services.exposure: No data on visitor care access or medication.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Occasional 'breaches of modesty' charges against non-gender-conforming presentation and same-sex couples; described as not widespread; state-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group not present; individual harassment common.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Sexual orientation as sensitive personal data (2023 law); constitution's privacy article.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Weak evidentiary base (single source) for the police-lever claim; military governance adds volatility but no documented trans-specific state campaign.

minors_guardians.exposure: No age- or minor-specific trans exposure documented; age-of-consent asymmetry was equalised in 2020.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Individual harassment described as common; societal stigmatisation; no trans-specific violence statistics against any background rate.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Constitution rejected re-criminalisation; state not documented as sponsor of group harassment.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Thin recourse (no gender-identity anti-discrimination protection; LGBTI groups cannot register) limits remedies if harassment occurs.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No gender-identity anti-discrimination law; no legal gender recognition; no documented trans-specific remedy or recourse mechanism.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Data-protection ground for sexual orientation (2023); constitutional privacy.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Resident-facing gaps per rubric are climate signals, but here they leave the visitor with no remedy if harassed or arrested.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.35-A features a universal, state-run register barring trans visitors with no effective remedy. This dossier documents no universal-exposure measure, no state targeting of trans people as a group, and repeal of the only recent criminalisation — materially lighter.

0.55-B documents discretionary secondary screening with administrative consequences and slow appeals. This case has a comparable tier of sporadic police misuse of neutral laws against presentation, plus documented common harassment and no recourse machinery — similar exposure tier, slightly wider uncertainty.

0.75-C shows working tribunals, compensation and release mechanisms tempering border discretion. This dossier documents no functioning trans-relevant remedy at all, and recent (2019) arrests with bribe extortion; that absence of recourse and volatility under military rule holds it below 0.75.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime is a lawful-but-fragile environment: no statute touches gender identity, same-sex conduct is lawful, and the constitution both added privacy protection and declined re-criminalisation. Against that, the record documents occasional police use of modesty charges against gender-nonconforming people, a history of arrests and bribe extortion within living memory of the law, common individual harassment, and no recourse machinery. Thin-data extrapolation from the governance character (military regime, rapid legislative swings, unregistered LGBTI groups) points to an elevated-tier outcome: an outed visitor faces harassment and possible police friction with modesty-charge misuse, not imprisonment, organised targeting or universal-exposure state measures. No border, custody, facility or care data tempers or aggravates this either way; the score reflects moderate police/social exposure with thin remedy.
